items.readable_text:
Content:
As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called constructive definitions of the form

Content:
[MATH: \big\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \big\}]

Content:
where the [MATH: {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}}] is an expression (or formula) that depends on a variable that constructs elements of our set when the variable runs over some [MATH: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}.]

Content:
For example, the set [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: A = \big\{ 2n+1\, : \, n\in\mathbb N_0 \big \}]

Content:
is defined constructively and contains all positive odd numbers:

Content:
[MATH: A|= {2n + 1: n ∈ N_{0}}; = {2(0) + 1, 2(1) + 1, 2(2) + 1, 2(3) + 1, …}; = {1, 3, 5, 7, …}]

Content:
Sometimes, it's helpful to write a set using a constructive definition. For example, how might we express the following set constructively?

Content:
[MATH: B = \big\{ 4, 7, 10, 13, \ldots \big\}]

Content:
First, notice that the elements of our set
[MATH: 4,\quad 7,\quad 10,\quad 13,\quad \ldots]
form an arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=3{:}]

Content:
[MATH: d|= 3; = 7 − 4; = 10 − 7; = 13 − 10; =⋮]

Content:
So, the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence for [MATH: n\in\mathbb N] is given by
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1) ⋅ d; = 4 + (n − 1) ⋅ 3; = 4 + 3n − 3; = 3n + 1.]

Content:
Therefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:

Content:
[MATH: B = \big\{ 3n+1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}]

Content:
The expression [MATH: 3n+1] generates the elements of our set when [MATH: n] runs over [MATH: \mathbb{N}.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- A bar "[MATH: \mid]" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. So, we could also express our set as follows:
[MATH: B=\big\{ 3n+1 \: \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}]
- The constructive definition of a given set is typically not unique. For example, we could also define [MATH: B] as follows:
[MATH: B=\big\{ 3n+4 \: :\: n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \big\}]
Notice that we used [MATH: \mathbb N_0] as the base set.

This definition does indeed generate all elements of [MATH: B{:}]
[MATH: {3n + 4: n ∈ N_{0}}|= {3(0) + 4, 3(1) + 4, 3(2) + 4, 3(3) + 4, …}; = {4, 7, 10, 13, …}; = B.]

sections.readable_text:
Describe the set [MATH: S=\{... , -5, -3, -1, 1, 3, ...\}] using a constructive definition.

Hint: Take [MATH: a_1 = 1] in the sequence that generates the elements of [MATH: S.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the elements of our set [MATH: \ldots, \quad -5, \quad -3, \quad -1, \quad 1, \quad 3, \quad \ldots] form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=2{:}]

[MATH: d|= 2; = − 3 − (− 5); = − 1 − (− 3); = 1 − (− 1); = ⋯]

Therefore, setting [MATH: a_1=1,] the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence for [MATH: n\in\mathbb{Z}] is given by [MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1) ⋅ d; = 1 + (n − 1) ⋅ 2; = 1 + 2n − 2; = 2n − 1.]

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

[MATH: S = \big\{2n-1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{Z}\big\}]

Watch Out!

The constructive definition of a set is typically not unique.

Since the elements of [MATH: A] are generated by a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence, we could have picked any term in our sequence as [MATH: a_1] when determining [MATH: a_n.] We selected [MATH: a_1 = 1] because this led to a nice, simple expression in our constructive definition.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the elements of our set [MATH: \ldots,\quad -36, \quad -6, \quad -1, \quad -\dfrac1{6}, \quad -\dfrac1{36}, \quad \ldots] form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio [MATH: r=\dfrac16{:}]

[MATH: r|= (1)/(6); = ((− 6)/(− 36)); = ((− 1)/(− 6)); = ((− (1)/(6)))/((− 1)); = ⋯]

Therefore, setting [MATH: a_1=-\dfrac16,] the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence for [MATH: n\in\mathbb{Z}] is given by

[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = (− (1)/(6)) ⋅ ((1)/(6))^{n − 1}; = − ((1)/(6)) ⋅ ((1)/(6))^{− 1} ⋅ ((1)/(6))^{n}; = − ((1)/(6))^{n}.]

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

[MATH: S = \left\{-\left(\dfrac16\right)^{n} \: : \: n\in \mathbb{Z}\right\}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called constructive definitions of the form

Content:
[MATH: \big\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \big\}]

Content:
where the [MATH: {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}}] is an expression (or formula) that depends on a variable that constructs elements of our set when the variable runs over some [MATH: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}.]

Content:
For example, the set [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: A = \big\{ 2n+1\, : \, n\in\mathbb N_0 \big \}]

Content:
is defined constructively and contains all positive odd numbers:

Content:
[MATH: A|= {2n + 1: n ∈ N_{0}}; = {2(0) + 1, 2(1) + 1, 2(2) + 1, 2(3) + 1, …}; = {1, 3, 5, 7, …}]

Content:
Sometimes, it's helpful to write a set using a constructive definition. For example, how might we express the following set constructively?

Content:
[MATH: B = \big\{ 4, 7, 10, 13, \ldots \big\}]

Content:
First, notice that the elements of our set
[MATH: 4,\quad 7,\quad 10,\quad 13,\quad \ldots]
form an arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=3{:}]

Content:
[MATH: d|= 3; = 7 − 4; = 10 − 7; = 13 − 10; =⋮]

Content:
So, the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence for [MATH: n\in\mathbb N] is given by
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1) ⋅ d; = 4 + (n − 1) ⋅ 3; = 4 + 3n − 3; = 3n + 1.]

Content:
Therefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:

Content:
[MATH: B = \big\{ 3n+1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}]

Content:
The expression [MATH: 3n+1] generates the elements of our set when [MATH: n] runs over [MATH: \mathbb{N}.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- A bar "[MATH: \mid]" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. So, we could also express our set as follows:
[MATH: B=\big\{ 3n+1 \: \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}]
- The constructive definition of a given set is typically not unique. For example, we could also define [MATH: B] as follows:
[MATH: B=\big\{ 3n+4 \: :\: n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \big\}]
Notice that we used [MATH: \mathbb N_0] as the base set.

This definition does indeed generate all elements of [MATH: B{:}]
[MATH: {3n + 4: n ∈ N_{0}}|= {3(0) + 4, 3(1) + 4, 3(2) + 4, 3(3) + 4, …}; = {4, 7, 10, 13, …}; = B.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence

Example Prompt:
Describe the set [MATH: S=\{... , -5, -3, -1, 1, 3, ...\}] using a constructive definition.

Hint: Take [MATH: a_1 = 1] in the sequence that generates the elements of [MATH: S.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that the elements of our set
[MATH: \ldots, \quad -5, \quad -3, \quad -1, \quad 1, \quad 3, \quad \ldots]
form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=2{:}]

[MATH: d|= 2; = − 3 − (− 5); = − 1 − (− 3); = 1 − (− 1); = ⋯]

Therefore, setting [MATH: a_1=1,] the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence for [MATH: n\in\mathbb{Z}] is given by
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1) ⋅ d; = 1 + (n − 1) ⋅ 2; = 1 + 2n − 2; = 2n − 1.]

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

[MATH: S = \big\{2n-1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{Z}\big\}]

Watch Out!

The constructive definition of a set is typically not unique.

Since the elements of [MATH: A] are generated by a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence, we could have picked any term in our sequence as [MATH: a_1] when determining [MATH: a_n.] We selected [MATH: a_1 = 1] because this led to a nice, simple expression in our constructive definition.

---

Item 5 — Example: Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence

Example Prompt:
Describe the set [MATH: S=\left\{\ldots, -36, -6, -1, -\dfrac1{6}, -\dfrac1{36}, ...\right\}] using a constructive definition.

Hint: Take [MATH: a_1 = -\dfrac16] in the sequence that generates the elements of [MATH: S.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that the elements of our set
[MATH: \ldots,\quad -36, \quad -6, \quad -1, \quad -\dfrac1{6}, \quad -\dfrac1{36}, \quad \ldots]
form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio [MATH: r=\dfrac16{:}]

[MATH: r|= (1)/(6); = ((− 6)/(− 36)); = ((− 1)/(− 6)); = ((− (1)/(6)))/((− 1)); = ⋯]

Therefore, setting [MATH: a_1=-\dfrac16,] the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence for [MATH: n\in\mathbb{Z}] is given by

[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = (− (1)/(6)) ⋅ ((1)/(6))^{n − 1}; = − ((1)/(6)) ⋅ ((1)/(6))^{− 1} ⋅ ((1)/(6))^{n}; = − ((1)/(6))^{n}.]

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

[MATH: S = \left\{-\left(\dfrac16\right)^{n} \: : \: n\in \mathbb{Z}\right\}]

---

Item 8 — Tutorial: Conditional Definitions of Sets

Content:
We can also define sets using so-called conditional definitions of the form

Content:
[MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{conditions}} \}]

Content:
where our set contains only those elements of the [MATH: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}] that satisfy the given [MATH: {\color{blue}\textrm{conditions}}] (or restrictions).

Content:
For example, the set [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: A = \{n\in \mathbb Z \::\: -2\leq n\leq 2\}]

Content:
is defined conditionally and contains all integers between [MATH: -2] and [MATH: 2] inclusive:

Content:
[MATH: A = \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}]

Content:
It's often helpful to describe sets using conditional definitions. For example, let's rewrite the following set using a conditional definition.

Content:
[MATH: S = \big\{50,51,52,53,\ldots\big\}]

Content:
The set [MATH: S] contains all natural numbers greater than or equal to [MATH: 50,] which we can write as follows:

Content:
[MATH: S = \{n\in \mathbb N \::\: n\geq 50\}]

Content:
The conditional definition of a set is not unique. We can write down an equivalent definition of [MATH: S] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: S = \{n\in \mathbb N \::\: n\gt 49\}]

Content:
Under this definition, [MATH: S] contains all natural numbers greater than [MATH: 49,] excluding [MATH: 49.]

Content:
Although [MATH: \mathbb N] is the most natural base set in this instance, we can also define [MATH: S] using the set of integers [MATH: \mathbb Z] as the base set. For example,

Content:
[MATH: S = \{n\in \mathbb Z \::\: n\geq 50\}.]

---

The set [MATH: S] contains all integer numbers between [MATH: -9] and [MATH: 5] (including [MATH: -9] and [MATH: 5]).

Therefore, the set can be written as

Note: This definition is not unique. For example, we can write [MATH: S] equivalently as follows:
[MATH: S = \big\{ x \in \mathbb Z \: : \: -10 \lt x \lt 6 \big\}]
